existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Gender in the making of class: a women's town and a men's town, Paris and Hanover, Ontario (1985–90)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985): 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations', with women's historians and historians of childhood, 'have reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42); 'Skill, too, is a socially constructed category' (pp. 42–43). Of the Marxist analysis in Women at Work, Ontario, 1850–1930 (1975) she writes, quoting feminist critics (n. 20: Phillips and Taylor; Hartmann), that it 'explains why a hierarchy of labour is necessary within the waged labour force, but tells us nothing about why women end up at the bottom of this hierarchy' (p. 43). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990; unread here) compares Paris and Hanover, Ontario. Heron, a labour historian, reviewing it (CHR, 1991, read in full): 'the most exhilarating, challenging book to appear in modern Canadian social history in many years'; it 'integrates and surpasses' women's, labour, technological and economic history, and 'Parr gives the boot to neo-classical analysis, simplistic Marxism, and radical feminism' (p. 218). He quotes its introduction that 'the parts and proportions of the social landscape covered by class and gender alter' (p. 10) but finds that in the 1949 Paris strike 'she has suppressed the impact of class where it was undeniably a crucial force' (p. 220). From her own figures he suggests that 'the portrait of the "women's town" may be slightly misleading' (p. 219). He also finds that she downplays the wars and the state and 'seldom makes any reference to the considerable Canadian literature on work, class, gender, or small-town life' (pp. 220–21). He concludes that she 'has pushed us onto new terrain where gender is neither ignored nor is it given a monocausal explanatory force' (p. 221). Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991) sees 'a more dynamic alternative to the old and stale studies that focused more on workers' industrial and organizational activities', while doubting conclusions drawn from 'the testimony of seven women' (p. 175). Dennis (EcHR, 1991) calls it 'an important contribution to the literature of labour history and locality studies' (p. 762). A contribution from inside the field's gender strand, alongside Sangster (1989) and Bradbury (1993). It does not claim that labour history lacked gender before 1990. edge_842 and edge_889 (cdn_women_gender → cdn_working_class) already carry the entry-level contribution and critique.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: British child immigrants as labouring children (1977–80), and childhood as a history of power (1985)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: In-period. Her Yale PhD (1977), 'The Home Children: British Juvenile Immigrants to Canada, 1868–1924', is recorded in the AHA Directory of History Dissertations (record 45612; adviser Robin Winks). Drystek's review of Labouring Children (Archivaria 11, 1980–81, read in full) names the thesis as the source of its sample of 997 Barnardo case histories (p. 241). He quotes the book's aims: a 'study of the life and work of child immigrants in Britain and Canada' (p. 13) that would 'reveal a darker side of evangelicalism, of turn-of-the-century childhood, and of Canadian rural life than the record has so far been allowed to express' (p. 12). His reading is critical: 'because of the authors' almost uniformly negative approach, the study is of limited value', the sample's statistical basis is unexplained, and 'the argument that a British child immigrant suffered a special burden is not convincing' (pp. 241–42). The book itself is unread here. Her own words (Atlantis, 1985) turn the subject into a question about power: she finds it troubling to treat women and children 'as part of one subject', admits to being 'part of a group who wrote, reviewed, lectured and squabbled this cluster into convention', and asks 'Is it nature which ties women and children together as subjects? Clearly not' (p. 39); the family 'is experienced by members of different generations in very different ways' (p. 44). She also edited Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982; title-level, see edge_792). A contribution among the field's early works, not its origin: Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) precedes it.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Disaggregating the sexual division of labour: gender and class compared across workplaces, read beyond Canada (1988–93)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the CSSH article of 1988 (first-page extract read, p. 511) observes that 'economists and feminist theorists have been interested in sexual divisions as general features of the economic or sex/gender system rather than as boundaries between tasks forged in defined contexts by particular clashes of interest', and that 'most analysts have dealt with gender division as a characteristic of the work force as a whole'. Reviews of The Gender of Breadwinners outside Canada (all read in full): Benson (JAH, 1993, p. 1630) writes that 'few historians have successfully integrated the discussion of these two fundamental relationships' and that 'Parr joins this small but growing group'. On p. 1631 Benson continues: 'Like others influenced by post-structuralist theory, she emphasizes the shifting and multivalent meanings often obscured by dualisms'; Parr 'gives gender and class coordinate roles in her analysis but downplays ethnicity'. Dennis (EcHR, 1991) finds that she 'goes far beyond previous accounts of connections between capitalism and patriarchy' (p. 761) but faults graphs that 'cavalierly use straight lines to connect a handful of isolated observations' (p. 762). Bertaux (JEH, 1992) wants 'a basic quantitative summary of work force data' (p. 240) but concludes that 'the topic of gender and work is not strictly a "women's issue"' (p. 241). The book itself is unread here. This records reception in international journals, not adoption. Optional: edge_840 (cdn_women_gender → gender) already links the Canadian field to the international entry.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Postwar Canadian consumption as a politics of nation, class and gender: domestic goods, designers and householders (1999)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: In-period, her own words: the abstract of 'Household Choices as Politics and Pleasure in 1950s Canada' (ILWCH 55, 1999, a special issue on class and consumption) reads 'How much consumption matters is a cultural difference, a shared national predicament, a politics grounded in the circumstances of class, and learned as a gendered responsibility', and asks 'When producers were not paramount in the regulation of consumption, to what priorities was commerce subsidiary?' Domestic Goods (1999) is unread here; as Brush quotes it (EH.NET, 2000, read in full), it is 'an archeology of the material, moral, and economic choices and constraints which formed Canadian commodity culture in the two decades after the Second World War' (p. 17). It asks 'How much can citizens talk back to manufacturers and the state about domestic goods?' (pp. 3–4). It sets itself against accounts that 'naturalize[d] these hortatory American norms as the intrinsic qualities of "consumer society"' (p. 11), and it places studies of material culture 'into unaccustomed company' (p. 3). Brush notes that Parr 'locates the history of consumption as a history primarily of women as consumers, in contrast to the male-dominated fields of design and manufacturing'. Criticism: Owram (BC Studies 129, 2001, read in full) finds the book's 'strength is in its parts rather than in some seamless thesis' (p. 103). He reads her as arguing that 'the assumption of consumer sovereignty is facile' (p. 104), and answers that 'Canadians, both men and women, preferred Fords to Volvos, and that is what they got' (p. 105). edge_843 (cdn_women_gender ↔ consumption, comparison) is title-level; this edge adds read evidence.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Embodied, sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change in Canada, 1953–2003 (2006–10)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Dated 2006–2011; no claim here concerns her work before 2000. Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (UBC Press, 2010) is unread here. As Jackson quotes it (Senses and Society 6:2, 2011, read in full), Parr seeks to move beyond 'representations . . . in language . . . , to open interpretive space in which to study the robust materiality of technologies, environments, and the everyday, to encounter them as directly and as fleshly as possible' (p. 9). Jackson describes chapters on the NATO base at Gagetown, nuclear power and heavy water on Lake Huron, the St Lawrence Seaway at Iroquois, the Columbia River reservoir and Walkerton's water, each read through a sense ('Smell and Risk', 'Taste and Expertise'). She adds that Parr counts proprioception, kinesthetics and proxemics among the senses (pp. 225–27). Jackson places the book in the UBC Press Nature/History/Culture series (p. 225). Rumiel (Left History 15:1, 2011, read in full) notes 'the people whose lives and senses of self had been transformed' by megaprojects (p. 189). She suggests that 'a comparative analysis of a related case in a Canadian Aboriginal or Inuit community' was a missed opportunity (p. 189). The environmental line begins earlier with 'Smells Like?: Sources of Uncertainty in the History of the Great Lakes Environment' (Environmental History 11:2, 2006; metadata only). A contribution: it records her later field, not influence on environmental history's formation.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Her two-town study (1990) and 1995 essay deconstructed skill and treated 'portraits of experience' as 'interpretations, reclamations of sensations', while keeping 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy' (as read by Sangster, 2000)
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Both Parr texts are unread (the existing Parr entry records the 1995 essay as known only through Iacovetta–Kealey and Sangster). Sangster 2000, read in full: the 'polar worlds of men's and women's work in small town Ontario' show 'the positive results of talking gender' (p. 151, citing The Gender of Breadwinners); Parr grouped with Tillotson, Mercedes Steedman and Creese as having 'deconstructed the notion of skill' while 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy are still in evidence, unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157); from the 1995 essay (p. 364) the sentence that portraits of experience 'were interpretations, reclamations of sensations which first had been organized, then claimed as experience' (p. 159, as quoted by Sangster). Moderate: a named reader's account.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.map_label: Gender, skill and experience in Canada, 1990–95

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Sangster objects that Parr groups feminist and antifeminist critics of gender history together (1996).
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: The criticism is confined to p. 240 n2 and its quoted passage; it does not reject Parr’s entire gender-history project.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Parr explicitly connects her questions about gender and class categories to Scott’s work on the politics of gender categories, among other named interlocutors.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Parr’s own introduction to The Gender of Breadwinners, printed p.9, relates the questions posed by her two town studies to Scott and Denise Riley, alongside Mary Poovey and R.W.Connell. This supports a bounded methodological resource, not exclusive derivation or identical conclusions. Selected introduction only; the whole book and cited works were not newly read. Original 1990 publication and later reprints/digital preview remain distinct.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Morton notes that Parr’s Labouring Children necessarily reconstructs childhood largely through adult evidence, limiting recovery of children’s own voices.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 2000 p. 33/n. 92 pairs Joy Parr’s Labouring Children (1980) with Neil Sutherland’s Children in English-Canadian Society (1976). Both retain credit; Morton calls the evidence limitation inevitable and places it within an otherwise positive assessment of feminist and family-history expansion. This is a qualified methodological limit, not rejection of Parr’s achievement or a claim to have read her full book.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Owram praises Parr’s individual studies but questions whether Domestic Goods sustains a coherent argument about consumer sovereignty and the rationality of Canadian choices.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 2001 review 103–105: distinguishes the restricted postwar market from later choices and consumers collectively from individual consumers. He credits Parr’s modernist-design and material-culture studies; disagreement is particular, not rejection of her work. The complete book remains unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Roediger uses Parr’s analysis of gender, class and breadwinner unionism to rethink racial identity and skilled workers’ masculinity.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 1993, 130–131/n12 groups Parr with Faue/Boydston as non-zero-sum identity resources; 137/n25 explicitly uses Parr’s breadwinner unionism alongside Taillon/Cooper. Specific methodological resource, no sole credit or mentoring; underlying Gender of Breadwinners 1990 unread.

existing_incident_edges_inspected.relationship: Iacovetta presents Parr’s analysis of masculinity, skill and Germanness as a model for connecting gender with ethnicity in immigrant labour history.
existing_incident_edges_inspected.evidence_note: Own 1997: 12 invokes Gender of Breadwinners while arguing that earlier manliness studies insufficiently linked masculinity and ethnicity; 4 separately praises Labouring Children as gender-conscious analysis. Bounded analytical resource for her historiographical argument, not every Parr thesis or original monograph checked. Existing group 958/1170 routes are not already a Parr→Iacovetta personal resource.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Childhood and family as historical subjects
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: The demography umbrella's strand on childhood evidence (Ariès; Pollock) and its household studies can be read alongside Canadian childhood and family history, which grew from social and family history (Parr, ed., 1982; Bradbury, ed., 1992) more than from family reconstitution. PhD context: 12 of 132 PhDs engaging this group cite Ariès (9% vs 3%; lift 2.96). Comparison; no descent from Ariès is asserted.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Canadian debates over gender as a category
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Pierson's 1991 essay opens on feminist historians' turn to deconstruction and discourse analysis, naming Scott's theory of gender as the most acclaimed example. Parr (1995) and the 1995–96 Left History exchange (Sangster; Iacovetta and Kealey; Dubinsky and Marks) argued over gender history and women's history; their citations are checked, and Sangster's own position is taken from her 2011 retrospect; the replies are read only as defences of gender history. PhD context: 64 of 328 PhDs engaging this group cite Scott (20% vs 9% of all; lift 2.12).

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Gender as a dimension of class and family economies
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Parr's comparison of a textile town where most wage earners were women with a furniture town challenges conventional views of the distinctiveness of gender and class roles (author's book page). Bradbury's Working Families (age, gender and family survival) and Sangster's Dreams of Equality (women on the left) are title-level. Contribution of gender analysis to labour history; it does not claim the new labour history lacked it entirely. PhD context: 130 of 287 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Canadian women's & gender history also engage Canadian working-class history (45%; lift 2.81), counted after removing shared anchors (Bradbury, Parr, Sangster). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Postwar domestic goods, magazines and households
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Parr's Domestic Goods (1999), Korinek's reading of Chatelaine (2000) and Fahrni's Household Politics (2005) place women and households at the centre of postwar consumption. Title-level only: none of these books was read, so the comparison is a teaching pointer to the consumption entry, not a claim about their arguments.

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Feminist challenge to a ‘masculinist’ working-class history
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Sangster (2000): feminist challenges to the initially ‘masculinist’ shape of working-class history, and later calls to integrate race and ethnicity, shifted the field’s narrative and paradigms, integrating gender more effectively though not completely into class formation. A critique that also remade the field (Parr 1990; Bradbury 1993).

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Scott's theory of gender is weighed in Canadian debates over discourse, experience and gender history
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Valverde's 1990 review essay in Labour/Le Travail, read in full, treats Scott's Gender and the Politics of History (with Riley) as a key work in 'the controversy about discourse theory'. She notes that poststructuralism had a 'bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)' and that 'in Canada' the debate was posed as 'a yes-or-no question'. She concludes that Scott 'deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow'. Pierson's 1991 essay on Canadian women's history opens on the turn to deconstruction, with Scott's theorising of gender as its most acclaimed example (opening read). Reference lists show Scott cited by Linda Kealey (1992), Pierson (1992) and Parr's 1995 CHR essay on gender history (OpenAlex metadata; texts unread). Limits: the evidence shows engagement and debate, not adoption. Valverde is sympathetic but critical. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) is a Canadian critique of the linguistic turn, but its treatment of Scott was not checked here. The 1995–96 Left History exchange is title-level and is not evidence that names Scott. PhD context: 64 of 120 Canadian History PhDs citing Scott engage this field (53%, lift 2.12); 39 engage childhood and youth (lift 3.21), and 49 working-class history (lift 1.87).
named_group_routes_inspected.map_label: Scott's gender theory in Canadian debates

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Eley and Nield dated gender's entry into ILWCH's field of vision to Scott's 1987 controversy; the debate developed alongside wider feminist revisions of class history — Canning (1992–96), Rose (1992), Clark (1995), Parr and Sangster in Canada — from which, they wrote, 'the study of class has benefited powerfully' (2000)
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Eley and Nield 2000, read in full: gender entered the journal's field of vision with Scott's 1987 controversy (p. 4); Katznelson–Zolberg 'notably missed gender entirely' (p. 4); Canning's work 'has disengaged class from the sovereignty of "objective" economic and social interests' (p. 8); 'the study of class has benefited powerfully from feminist revisions' (p. 8, n. 24 naming Clark, Rose, Baron, Frader and Rose). Sangster 2000 (read in full), pp. 151, 157, on Parr and the Canadian feminists. Rose: UC Press description only; Clark: existing record. The gender entry's own strands keep each author's work; this arrow records the debate's bearing on the field.
named_group_routes_inspected.map_label: Gender and the making of class, 1987–2000

named_group_routes_inspected.relationship: Canadian debates included Palmer's materialist critique (1987–90), Valverde's sympathetic criticism of poststructuralist gender history (1990–95), Parr's gendered study of work (1990–95) and Sangster's materialist feminism (2000)
named_group_routes_inspected.evidence_note: Sangster 2000, pp. 157–161 (read in full): the question 'whether we are simply replacing working-class history's failings concerning gender, with a linguistic approach that obscures class' (p. 157); Valverde cited for 'a certain logic carrying one from the (more generally accepted) deconstruction of notions of "male/female" skill to a complete deconstruction of class' (p. 158); 'Dismissing the "new" labour history as "mechanistic" marxism conflates diverse traditions of materialism' (p. 160 n. 121). Valverde 1990 (existing reading); Palmer's book through the Temple page and Callinicos. The existing strand cdn_working_class/state_of_the_field_2000 covers Palmer, Morton and Sangster from the Canadian field's side; this arrow records the debate's entry into it.
